# Learning Objectives for Today's Class

- Describe the **analytics journey** and the role of **business intelligence (BI)** within it.

- Differentiate between **structured**, **semi-structured**, and **unstructured** data.

- Map **real-world data sources** to appropriate **data types**.

# The Analytics Journey: Pre-Analytics [2]

- **Pre-Analytics/Data Management:** where one attempts to **extract** the needed
*data* for analysis.  Data can either be:
.div[
.pull-left[
## .center[.large[.large[.large[`r emo::ji("canned_food")`]]]]
* Stale, uninteresting, convenient
* Highly processed and archived
* Example: `iris`, `mtcars`, `titanic`
]
.pull-right[
## .center[.large[.large[.large[`r emo::ji("tomato")`]]]]
* Fresh, interesting, challenging
* Impactful
* Examples: [Cincinnati Open Data Portal](https://data.cincinnati-oh.gov/),
[Ohio Data Portal](https://data.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/data/), [US Government's Open Data](https://www.data.gov/).
]
]

.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>

While highly processed data can be useful for learning basic concepts, **real-world (often messy) data are much more interesting to work with** — e.g., we can make useful and meaningful decisions from them, as you just did. In this class, we will learn how to scrape, extract, and clean messy data in addition to visualizing clean[ed] data.

**Source:** Slide inspired by Earo Wang's "What I mean by data" (STATS 220, University of Auckland; site no longer online).
]

# The Analytics Journey: Descriptive [1]

```{r extract_crashes, cache=TRUE, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
crashes = readr::read_csv('../../data/cincy_2025_crashes.csv') |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    datetime = lubridate::ymd_hms(crashdate),
    date = lubridate::as_date(datetime),
    hour = lubridate::hour(datetime)
  )

# one row per crash; recompute the weekday from the crash date so every
# slide uses the same definition (the raw dayofweek strings use inconsistent
# abbreviations across data vintages, e.g. TUE vs TUES)
unique_crashes = crashes |>
  dplyr::distinct(instanceid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(date)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dayofweek = lubridate::wday(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE, week_start = 1),
    weather = forcats::as_factor(weather)
  )
```

**Descriptive Analytics:** where one attempts to **understand** the data through **descriptive statistics** and **visualizations**.

### Descriptive Statistics for 2 Categorical Variables (one row per *crash*)

.small[

```{r desc_stats, echo=FALSE}
unique_crashes |>
  dplyr::select(dayofweek, weather) |>
  purrr::map(.f = table)
```

]


---

# The Analytics Journey: Descriptive [2]

**Descriptive Analytics:** where one attempts to **understand** the data through **descriptive statistics** and **visualizations**.

### A Simple Visualization - A Bar Chart of Crashes Per Day

```{r viz, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.25}
unique_crashes |>
  dplyr::count(dayofweek) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = n, y = forcats::fct_rev(dayofweek))) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = miamired) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = scales::comma(n)), hjust = -0.15, size = 2.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12)),
                              labels = scales::comma) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = 'Count/Freq', y = 'Day of the Week',
       title = 'Crashes by Day in Cincinnati in 2025',
       caption = 'Created by: Fadel Megahed | Data source: City of Cincy Open Data Portal (rvmt-pkmq)')
```

---

# The Analytics Journey: Descriptive [3]

**Descriptive Analytics:** where one attempts to **understand** the data through **descriptive statistics** and **visualizations**.

```{r viz2a, echo=FALSE, cache=TRUE, fig.height=2.85}
daily_crashes_2025 = unique_crashes |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(date), lubridate::year(date) == 2025) |>
  dplyr::count(date) |>
  tidyr::complete(
    date = seq(as.Date('2025-01-01'), as.Date('2025-12-31'), by = 'day'),
    fill = list(n = 0)
  )

cal = calendR::calendR(
  title = NULL,
  year = 2025,
  special.days = daily_crashes_2025$n,
  orientation = "landscape",
  day.size = 2,
  months.size = 8,
  weeknames.size = 3,
  margin = 0,
  text.size = 8,
  title.size = 14,
  gradient = TRUE,
  low.col = "#FFFFED",
  special.col = miamired,
  legend.pos = 'right',
  legend.title = '# Crashes') +
  ggplot2::theme(
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = 'bold', color =  miamired),
    legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = 'bold', size = 9),
    legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 7),
    plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(size = 7)
    ) +
  ggplot2::labs(caption = 'Created by: Fadel Megahed | Data source: City of Cincy Open Data Portal (rvmt-pkmq)')

cal

```

# The Analytics Journey: Continued

.pull-left[
### Predictive Analytics

## .center["What *will* happen?"]

- **Statistical/ML models** trained on historical data.

- Only as good as the data behind them — start simple.
]

--

.pull-right[
### Prescriptive Analytics

## .center["What *should* we do?"]

- Models that recommend **actions**, not just forecasts.

- e.g., which drivers should a trucking company flag for safety interventions — and at what cost?
]

# Business Intelligence: From Data to Decisions

# What is Business Intelligence?

> "... to enable **interactive access (sometimes in real time)** to data, to enable manipulation of data, and to give business managers and analysts the ability to conduct appropriate analysis.
By analyzing ... data, situations, and performances, decision makers get valuable insights that enable them to **make more informed and better decisions** ... BI is based on the **transformation of data to information, then to decisions, and finally to actions.**"

```{r bin_paper, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="A schematic of an interactive BI tool for stock market prediction", out.width="55%"}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/stock_market.JPG")
```

.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>

**Quote** from Sharda, R., Delen, D., & Turban, E. (2013). Business Intelligence: A managerial perspective on analytics. Prentice Hall Press.

**Image Credit:** Joint work with Bin Weng.
]

# One Job Ad, Three Shapes [1]: Unstructured

<span style="display:inline-block; background:#e2e2f9; color:#3d3d80; font-weight:700; font-size:12px; padding:3px 12px; border-radius:10px; text-transform:uppercase;">Unstructured</span> &nbsp; **Research Data Scientist, Magic Eye** at Google (Mountain View, CA; posted 2026-08-12). This is what a human, or Job Scout, actually reads:

<div style="height:380px; overflow-y:auto; background:#F5F5F5; border:1px solid #d1d5db; border-radius:6px; padding:10px 16px; font-size:12.5px; line-height:1.45; white-space:pre-wrap; font-family: Georgia, serif;">MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS:

 * Master's degree in Statistics, Data Science, Mathematics, Physics, Economics, Operations Research, Engineering, or a related quantitative field.
 * 3 years of work experience using analytics to solve product or business problems, coding (e.g., Python, R, SQL), querying databases or statistical analysis, or a PhD degree.

PREFERRED QUALIFICATIONS:

 * 5 years of work experience using analytics to solve product or business problems, coding (e.g., Python, R, SQL), querying databases or statistical analysis, or a PhD degree.

ABOUT THE JOB:

Magic Eye's mission is to guide strategic decision making for Google's consumer products through data-informed insights, actionable user metrics, and definitions of success. The analysis team partners closely with cross-product area teams from Search, Ads, Android, YouTube, etc., and cross-functionally with teams from Engineering, Behavioral Economics, UX, Finance to bring methodology, data, and insights to Googlers and Google leads. [...] Key research questions include understanding the rapidly evolving GenAI landscape and user journeys across products and devices to identify cross-company strategic opportunities.

Individual pay is determined by factors including job-related skills, experience, and relevant education or training.

US: $147000 - $210000 (USD) + 15% bonus target + equity + benefits

RESPONSIBILITIES:

 * Collaborate with stakeholders in cross-projects and team settings to identify and clarify business or product questions to answer. [...]</div>

.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>

**Unstructured** data is free text with no fixed fields. Notice the **salary is in there** ($147K to $210K): the information exists, but no filter or chart can reach it until someone (or some model) extracts it.
]

# One Job Ad, Three Shapes [2]: Semi-Structured

<span style="display:inline-block; background:#fef5c4; color:#7a6210; font-weight:700; font-size:12px; padding:3px 12px; border-radius:10px; text-transform:uppercase;">Semi-Structured</span> &nbsp; Job Scout's AI model reads that text and emits **JSON**: tagged, nested, machine-readable, but with a flexible shape.

.pull-left[

<div style="height:340px; overflow-y:auto; background:#111827; color:#e5e7eb; border-radius:6px; padding:12px 16px; font-size:12px; line-height:1.5; white-space:pre; font-family: Consolas, Menlo, monospace;">[
  {"skillId": "python",     "importance": "required"},
  {"skillId": "r",          "importance": "required"},
  {"skillId": "sql",        "importance": "required"},
  {"skillId": "statistical_analysis",
                            "importance": "required"},
  {"skillId": "data_analysis",
                            "importance": "required"},
  {"skillId": "stakeholder_management",
                            "importance": "required"},
  {"skillId": "data_wrangling",
                            "importance": "required"},
  {"skillId": "causal_inference",
                            "importance": "preferred"},
  {"skillId": "experimental_design",
                            "importance": "preferred"},
  {"skillId": "generative_ai",
                            "importance": "preferred"},
  {"skillId": "mathematics","importance": "preferred"},
  {"skillId": "operations_research",
                            "importance": "preferred"}
]</div>

]

.pull-right[

.font90[

- **Semi-structured** data carries its own labels (`skillId`, `importance`) but records can differ: this ad has 12 skills, another has 4.

- This is what **APIs** return (JSON like this, or XML/HTML). We'll learn to request and parse it in weeks 4 and 5.

- The *required*/*preferred* labels were decided by an AI model reading the ad: extraction adds structure **and** assumptions.

]

]

---

# One Job Ad, Three Shapes [3]: Structured

<span style="display:inline-block; background:#d9edc2; color:#3d5c14; font-weight:700; font-size:12px; padding:3px 12px; border-radius:10px; text-transform:uppercase;">Structured</span> &nbsp; The clean record lands as **one row** in the `scout_postings` table, with the same fields for every posting:

<table style="margin: 8px auto 0; border-collapse: collapse; font-size: 14px; min-width: 62%;">
  <tr style="background:#f3f4f6;"><th style="text-align:left; padding:5px 14px; border-bottom:2px solid #d1d5db;">Field</th><th style="text-align:left; padding:5px 14px; border-bottom:2px solid #d1d5db;">Value</th></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">source</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">activejobs</td></tr>
  <tr style="background:#f9fafb;"><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">title</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">Research Data Scientist, Magic Eye</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">company</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">Google</td></tr>
  <tr style="background:#f9fafb;"><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">location_city, location_state</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">Mountain View, CA</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">remote</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">0</td></tr>
  <tr style="background:#f9fafb;"><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">category</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">fulltime</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">posted_at</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">2026-08-12</td></tr>
  <tr style="background:#f9fafb;"><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">active</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">1</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:4px 14px; font-family:monospace; color:#c3142d;">visa_sponsorship</td><td style="padding:4px 14px;">unknown</td></tr>
</table>

.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>

**Structured** data is rows &times; columns with identical fields throughout. This is the *only* shape the dashboard's filters and charts can use. Notice what didn't survive the trip: there is no `salary` column.
]

class: table80

# From Data to Decisions: The BI Value Chain

.pull-left[
### The Journey

| Stage | Question | Output |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **Data** | What happened? | Raw facts |
| **Information** | What does it mean? | Context + structure |
| **Knowledge** | Why did it happen? | Patterns + insights |
| **Decision** | What should we do? | Action |
]

--

.pull-right[
### Example: Job Market

| Stage | Example |
|:---:|:---|
| **Data** | 1,437 postings harvested by Job Scout |
| **Information** | SQL is tagged in 31% of postings; communication in 79% |
| **Knowledge** | Employers want the *pairing*: technical skills **and** the ability to explain findings |
| **Decision** | Build both this semester: code every week, present your results |
]


---
class: inverse, center, middle

# So What is Data Visualization?

---

# What is Data Visualization?

Data visualization involves **presenting data in a graphical format**. It is really a process that starts by getting data, creating initial plot(s) and modifying them to answer questions of interest. **A good chart takes time and iteration** — for example, see [Cedric Scherer's visualization of the UNESCO data on global student to teacher ratios](https://www.cedricscherer.com/2019/05/17/the-evolution-of-a-ggplot-ep.-1/).

```{r data_viz_gif, echo=FALSE, out.width='58%', interval=100, aniopts="controls"}
knitr::include_graphics('https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/1e7033393a2c70dc1255c5d0f1c563e945519251/61035/img/evol-ggplot/evol-ggplot-1.gif')
```

---

# The Goals of Data Visualization

- **Record** information

  * Sometimes a well-designed [interactive table](https://flourish.studio/blog/how-make-interactive-table/) *is* the best visualization

- **Analyze** data to support reasoning

  * Develop and assess hypotheses (EDA)

  * Reveal patterns

  * Discover errors in data

- **Communicate** ideas to others

  * Infographics, statistical charts, interactive charts, dashboards

- **Interact with the data (which supports all the above)**

  * You just did this — filtering, mapping, and drilling into the Job Market Explorer

---

# Analyze Data: The 1854 Cholera Outbreak

```{r cholera_outbreak, echo=FALSE, out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../figures/cholera.jpg')
```


.footnote[
<html>
<hr>
</html>

Note the **encoding**: each death is a mark whose **position** on the map carries the information — and we perceive position more accurately than other encoding channels.

Source: Leskovec, J., Rajaraman, A., & Ullman, J. D. (2020). Mining of Massive Data Sets (Third Edition). Cambridge University Press.  Image is from Chapter 1, which can be accessed [here](http://infolab.stanford.edu/~ullman/mmds/ch1n.pdf).
]

# Recap

---

# Summary of Main Points

By now, you should be able to do the following:

- Describe the **analytics journey** (pre-analytics, descriptive, predictive, prescriptive) and the role of **BI** within it.

- Differentiate between **structured**, **semi-structured**, and **unstructured** data — and recognize all three inside one real pipeline.

- Map **real-world data sources** (CSVs, APIs, web pages, free text) to appropriate **data types**.

**Skills you practiced along the way:** identifying the **unit of analysis** (rows ≠ crashes!), distinguishing **counts from rates**, questioning **data provenance**, and reading a chart's **visual encodings**.
